| [THEORY-036](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-036.md) | Dennett's real-pattern criterion, compressibility against the bit map, admits almost every non-random pattern; the projectibility, perspective and scale-relativity that rainforest realism needs are later additions that do the ontological work | Dennett (1991), [LIT-220](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-220.md) — a pattern is real "if there is a description of the data that is more efficient than the bit map, whether or not anyone can concoct it". | [THEORY-058](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-058.md) | Mental disorders are maintained by self-reinforcing causal loops rather than expressing a latent common cause, which is how they can outlast their triggers | Three traditions that do not cite one another for it put self-sustaining loops where a latent cause would be. Borsboom ([LIT-547](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-547.md)) makes disorder an alternative stable state of a strongly connected symptom network, kept up by hysteresis after its trigger has gone. Salkovskis, Sighvatsson and Sigurdsson ([LIT-538](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-538.md)) make it a threat meaning protected by the behaviour it drives. Kendler ([LIT-539](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-539.md)) finds causal loops across levels, from genes to culture. The convergence is real; the evidence is indirect, simulated or clinical, and none of it is an individual time series showing hysteresis, so the account is Proposed. It says nothing about what starts a disorder. | Proposed |
